Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen RaaS 'gentlemen*' scheduled-task creation/execution · [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop/ThrottleBlood.sys load & GentlemenCollection staging · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] The Gentlemen SystemBC / Cobalt Strike C2 beacon to named infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] The Gentlemen cross-platform encryptor execution by known hash · [LLM] wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs (anti-forensics) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen RaaS 'gentlemen*' scheduled-task creation/execution AIInstallation High
Hunts creation, deletion or execution of any Windows scheduled task whose name matches the string 'gentlemen*', the article's explicit high-severity SIEM signal for The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS staging its Go payloads. This is a campaign-unique naming convention rather than a generic schtasks abuse pattern. Rationale: Uses the article's single most specific string — the 'gentlemen*' scheduled-task name that Unit 42 recommends alerting on directly — bound to schtasks.exe / Task Scheduler event IDs so it fires on create, delete or execute. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation task legitimately named after a project called 'gentlemen'
  • Red-team/purple-team exercise replaying The Gentlemen TTPs
  • A backup or monitoring vendor task whose GUID/description coincidentally tokenises to gentlemen (very rare)
  • Analyst re-running the IOC in a lab that writes the task to the same host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks command line and the parent process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) — confirm the task name literally starts with 'gentlemen' and note the payload path it launches. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender/EDR, delete the scheduled task, and quarantine the referenced binary; capture the task XML before deletion. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same task name, for GentlemenCollection staging folders, ThrottleBlood.sys/ThrottleStop.sys driver loads, and outbound SystemBC C2 to 45.86.230.112 to scope lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID in (4698,4699,4702) and EventData has "gentlemen")
    or (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "gentlemen")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware gentlemen-named Scheduled Task
id: 8f3c1e2a-4b7d-4a9c-9f21-0a1b2c3d4e5f
description: Detects creation or execution of a scheduled task whose name matches the string gentlemen*, a naming convention used by The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'gentlemen'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate tasks that coincidentally contain the token gentlemen (rare)
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*gentlemen* OR *Gentlemen* OR *GENTLEMEN*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/gentlemen/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\$$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\$$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop/ThrottleBlood.sys load & GentlemenCollection staging AIInstallation High
Hunts the GentleKiller EDR-killer framework: the load of the CVE-2025-7771 vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys driver (renamed ThrottleBlood.sys by the actor) and/or files dropped into the GentlemenCollection staging directory. Both are corroborated by Securelist/Kaspersky and Check Point/Dark Atlas as Gentlemen-specific defense-impairment tooling. Rationale: Anchors on the article's CVE-2025-7771 ThrottleStop.sys driver plus the externally-confirmed ThrottleBlood.sys rename and GentlemenCollection staging path — driver/file names unique enough that a load is high-fidelity BYOVD rather than benign CPU tuning. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/av-killer-exploiting-throttlestop-sys/117026/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-7771 • https://darkatlas.io/blog/how-a-go-binary-locks-down-enterprise-networks-in-minutes-the-story-behind-gentlemen-ransomware
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate TechPowerUp ThrottleStop CPU undervolting tool on an engineer/gaming laptop loading throttlestop.sys
  • Overclocking utility bundle installed by an enthusiast user
  • Security research VM intentionally loading the vulnerable driver for analysis
  • A folder legitimately named GentlemenCollection unrelated to the actor (unlikely)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\TechPowerUp\ThrottleStop\" and FileName =~ "throttlestop.sys")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the loading process and signer — benign use is the signed TechPowerUp ThrottleStop.exe; a ThrottleBlood.sys rename or load from a temp/GentlemenCollection path is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash via WDAC/ASR, and force full EDR scan; if the driver was loaded, treat AV/EDR on that host as compromised. 3) Hunt: enumerate processes killed around the load time, look for the gentlemen* scheduled task, SystemBC C2, and encryptor hashes; add ThrottleStop.sys to the Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist fleet-wide.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("throttlestop.sys","throttleblood.sys") or FolderPath has "GentlemenCollection"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("throttlestop.sys","throttleblood.sys")
    or TargetFilePath has "GentlemenCollection"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen SystemBC / Cobalt Strike C2 beacon to named infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on outbound connections to The Gentlemen's confirmed C2 IPs — SystemBC SOCKS5 node 45.86.230.112 plus 193.233.202.17 and 77.110.122.137, and the Cobalt Strike fallback 91.107.247.163. IPs cross-checked against Check Point/Dark Atlas SystemBC C2 reporting, not just the original article. Rationale: Uses the article's three C2 IPs plus the externally-confirmed SystemBC node 45.86.230.112 and Cobalt Strike fallback 91.107.247.163; direct IOC hits on known-bad infrastructure are inherently high-fidelity and warrant alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/systembc-c2-server-reveals-1570-victims.html • https://darkatlas.io/blog/how-a-go-binary-locks-down-enterprise-networks-in-minutes-the-story-behind-gentlemen-ransomware
ATT&CKT1071 T1090 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A C2 IP recycled to a legitimate VPS customer after infrastructure takedown
  • Threat-intel/sandbox appliance intentionally reaching the IP for enrichment
  • Security scanner probing the address range from a corporate egress point
  • Researcher pivoting on the IOC from a managed jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — SystemBC often runs as socks.exe and Cobalt Strike fallback via rundll32.exe; capture the process tree and any parent scheduled task. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate the beaconing host, and kill/quarantine the initiating binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process hash across the fleet, check for GentlemenCollection staging and ThrottleBlood.sys loads on the same host, and review DNS/proxy for adjacent SystemBC infrastructure and non-standard-port egress from servers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.86.230.112","193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","91.107.247.163")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.86.230.112","193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","91.107.247.163")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen cross-platform encryptor execution by known hash AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on execution or drop of the four SHA256 and four SHA1 hashes attributed to The Gentlemen's C/Go encryptors. Hash-based, so it is the most precise impact-phase signal for confirming detonation on Windows or ESXi-adjacent Windows management hosts. Rationale: Directly uses the eight article-supplied encryptor hashes (4x SHA256, 4x SHA1); hash matches leave no ambiguity, making this a critical confirm-detonation alert across process-create and file-write telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in a monitored sandbox host
  • IR team re-running the encryptor hash on a rebuild/test VM
  • Threat-intel platform hashing the file during ingestion (file-open, not execution)
  • Hash collision — effectively impossible for SHA256, negligible for SHA1
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ActionType is an execution/drop (not a benign file-hash-open by an AV), and identify the host and initiating account. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host and any hosts it has SMB/SSH sessions to, kill the process, and preserve a memory image; begin ransomware IR — assume encryption in progress. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and ESXi management hosts for the same hashes, for vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion, and for the SystemBC C2 to bound blast radius; validate offline backups.
let iocSha256 = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67","51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2","025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a","3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235"]);
let iocSha1 = dynamic(["8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d","d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2","5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3","a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ (iocSha256) or SHA1 in~ (iocSha1)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocSha256 = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67","51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2","025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a","3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235"]);
let iocSha1 = dynamic(["8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d","d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2","5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3","a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);

wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs (anti-forensics) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of wevtutil.exe clearing the Security or System event logs, the article's named defense-evasion signal used by The Gentlemen to erase tracks after EDR impairment. Also covers Security-log 1102 audit-cleared events. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit 'wevtutil to clear Security/System logs' recommendation, scoped to the clear-log verb plus the Security/System targets so it flags anti-forensic wiping rather than benign log queries. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gentlemen-ransomware-global-attacks/
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing a noisy System log during troubleshooting
  • SCCM/Intune or GPO maintenance script rotating logs
  • Imaging/sysprep pipeline clearing logs before capture
  • Backup software resetting event channels post-restore
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who ran wevtutil and the parent process — legitimate admin activity has a human/console parent; ransomware chains it after driver loads or scheduled-task execution. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the clear correlates with other Gentlemen IOCs; preserve any forwarded/SIEM copies of the cleared logs. 3) Hunt: check for preceding EDR tamper events, ThrottleBlood.sys loads, and gentlemen* tasks on the same host, and confirm whether Windows Event Forwarding retained the wiped records.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log") and CommandLine has_any ("Security","System"))
    or EventID == 1102
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Event Log Cleared via wevtutil (The Gentlemen Anti-Forensics)

description: Detects wevtutil.exe clearing the Security or System event log, a defense-evasion step used by The Gentlemen RaaS.

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\wevtutil.exe OR *\WEVTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:((*" cl "* OR *clear-log*) AND (*Security* OR *System*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\wevtutil\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\b(cl|clear-log)\b/i CommandLine=/(Security|System)/ | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner, the network-mapping tool the article names as frequently used by The Gentlemen for internal recon before lateral movement. Matches on the binary name and Famatech product metadata to catch renamed copies. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly-named Advanced IP Scanner recon tool, matched on binary name plus Famatech metadata to survive renames; kept at hunting tier because legit IT admins also use it. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gentlemen-ransomware-global-attacks/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/network admin running Advanced IP Scanner for legitimate subnet inventory
  • Helpdesk technician locating a device on the LAN
  • MSP onboarding scan of a new client network
  • Pentest/red-team engagement with authorized recon
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-netops","svc-itasset")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing account and host are not sanctioned IT admins, and check the launch time against other suspicious activity on the host. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and disable the account pending review; capture the scan output if written to disk. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on SMB writes to admin shares, SSH to ESXi hosts, the gentlemen* task, and SystemBC C2 from the same host to determine whether recon progressed to lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("advanced_ip_scanner.exe","advanced_port_scanner.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName in~ ("advanced_ip_scanner.exe","advanced_port_scanner.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Famatech"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("advanced_ip_scanner.exe","advanced_port_scanner.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

SecurityEvent

   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"

status: experimental
description: |

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

author: Clankerusecase

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

[GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8: TSDProxy: Internal proxy auth token forwarded to backend services enables management API escalation

TSDProxy: Internal proxy auth token forwarded to backend services enables management API escalation

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] TSDProxy management-API auth bypass: spoofed x-tsdproxy-id replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy internal auth token (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) captured/handled in host process command line
TSDProxy internal auth token (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) captured/handled in host process command line AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the TSDProxy internal per-process secret header 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token' appearing in any process command line on a host running tsdproxy or a proxied backend. This header is injected server-side into upstream requests only and must never surface in a shell; its presence in process telemetry indicates a compromised backend has captured the token to replay against the management API (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8). Rationale: 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token' is a unique internal-only header constant (consts.HeaderAuthToken) that TSDProxy sets exclusively on server-to-backend requests; it should never appear in a user-space process command line, making its presence a near-zero-FP signal of token capture. Anchored directly on the advisory PoC's token-exfiltration step. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy • https://medium.com/@sylvesterranjithfrancis/authentication-at-the-edge-the-identity-aware-proxy-pattern-and-the-one-header-that-gets-you-633cc2b6a2d2
ATT&CKT1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer inspecting or debugging forwarded proxy identity headers on the host
  • CI/integration test harness that echoes or asserts on request headers
  • A monitoring/health-check script that dumps HTTP request headers from the backend
  • TSDProxy verbose/debug logging that echoes request headers into stdout captured as a process arg
Suppression filter
// Exclude known CI/ops accounts that legitimately inspect headers
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("ci-runner","monitoring")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host runs tsdproxy or a backend it proxies; pull the full process tree and parent (InitiatingProcess) — a web/app service account spawning curl/wget/python handling this header is high-confidence compromise. 2) Contain: treat the TSDProxy auth token as burned — upgrade to >= 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e and restart tsdproxy to regenerate the per-process token; isolate the backend host. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 for replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/, and review tsdproxy management activity for proxy restart/pause, config enumeration, and outbound webhook deliveries (SSRF).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TSDProxy management-API auth bypass: spoofed x-tsdproxy-id replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the exploitation step of GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8: a localhost request carrying an attacker-controlled 'x-tsdproxy-id' identity header to the TSDProxy management API (127.0.0.1:8080, /api/v1/ paths). The management server trusts x-tsdproxy-id from localhost once a valid forwarded token is presented, so this pattern is the privilege escalation to full admin control (enumerate proxies, restart/pause services, trigger webhook SSRF). Rationale: Combines the spoofed-identity header 'x-tsdproxy-id' (attacker-supplied per the PoC: 'x-tsdproxy-id: attacker') with the fixed management endpoint 127.0.0.1:8080 / /api/v1/proxies from the advisory. Legitimate management calls arrive over Tailscale, not as a localhost request forging the identity header, so the combination is a high-fidelity escalation signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy • https://medium.com/@sylvesterranjithfrancis/authentication-at-the-edge-the-identity-aware-proxy-pattern-and-the-one-header-that-gets-you-633cc2b6a2d2
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually calling the local management API from the host for ops/troubleshooting
  • Local health-check or readiness probe hitting /api/v1/ on 127.0.0.1:8080
  • CI/automation that enumerates proxy config against the management port
  • A load test or debugging session that manually injects x-tsdproxy-id to test identity handling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","ci-runner") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","curl","wget","python","python3")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process/account — a proxied backend service account (not an interactive admin) issuing a loopback request to 127.0.0.1:8080 with a forged x-tsdproxy-id is confirmed exploitation; capture the id value and target /api/v1 path. 2) Contain: rotate the TSDProxy token by upgrading to >= 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e and restarting; block backend egress to the management port (network-namespace/firewall). 3) Hunt: review management-API actions in the same window for proxy restart/pause (DoS), full proxy enumeration, and configured-webhook deliveries (SSRF); correlate with UC1 token-capture hits on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan Electron app spawns shell/LOLBin child (attribute-view XSS to nodeIntegration RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE tail of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-44670: a stored XSS in SiYuan's attribute-view cell renderer runs in an Electron renderer with nodeIntegration:true and invokes require('child_process').exec, causing the SiYuan.exe process to spawn cmd/powershell/LOLBins. A note-taking Electron app spawning a command interpreter is highly anomalous. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete RCE mechanism (Electron nodeIntegration:true + require('child_process')) and the confirmed process boundary SiYuan.exe->interpreter; corroborated by GitLab advisory for the sibling CVE-2026-44670 and the DailyCVE writeup showing require('child_process').exec('calc') as the canonical payload. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://dailycve.com/siyuan-stored-xss-to-rce-critical/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan in-app auto-update spawning a helper/installer process
  • User invoking SiYuan 'open in default app' / 'reveal in explorer' which can spawn rundll32.exe FileProtocolHandler
  • SiYuan export features shelling out to a converter (e.g. pandoc) if bundled in the app dir
  • Security tooling injecting into SiYuan.exe and appearing as the parent of a scan process
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "rundll32.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "FileProtocolHandler")
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pandoc","siyuan-update","Squirrel"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; a benign hit is SiYuan opening a URL/file (rundll32 FileProtocolHandler). Any cmd/powershell with encoded/download/exec content is a true positive. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host in Defender, kill the SiYuan.exe process tree, and quarantine the workspace's data/storage/av/*.json files so they don't re-sync the payload. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate every device syncing the same SiYuan workspace/repo — the malicious AV cell propagates to all peers and fires on panel open; sweep those hosts for the same SiYuan.exe->interpreter spawn and for second-stage network egress.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "siyuan"   // SiYuan.exe Electron renderer/main
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\SiYuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan attribute-view JSON write followed by SiYuan shell spawn (storage-to-execution) AIInstallation Medium
Links the persisted CVE-2026-50551 payload to its trigger: a write to data\storage\av\<avID>.json (the backing store for attribute-view cells, planted via workspace sync) followed within minutes by SiYuan.exe spawning a shell/LOLBin when a victim opens the block-attribute panel. Bridges the persistence artifact to the RCE. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact backing-store path data/storage/av/<avID>.json plus the SiYuan.exe->interpreter execution boundary, correlated in a tight window so it fires only when a persisted cell precedes an RCE spawn — far higher fidelity than av-JSON writes alone (which SiYuan produces constantly). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate heavy database editing writes av/*.json seconds before an unrelated SiYuan-spawned helper process
  • SiYuan auto-update coinciding with routine av/*.json sync writes
  • Sysmon file-event volume causing a benign av write to fall inside the 5-minute window of a link-open rundll32 spawn
  • Backup/sync agents rewriting the whole workspace including av/*.json around app launch
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd has_any ("require('child_process')","require(\"child_process\")","-enc","-EncodedCommand","DownloadString","http") or ChildImage has_any ("certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Retrieve the AVFile and the child ProcessCommandLine; open the JSON and grep for HTML breakout markers (</textarea>, <img, onerror=, onload=, onmouseenter=). Presence of those strings in a cell that preceded a shell spawn confirms the chain. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the SiYuan tree, and pull/quarantine the offending av JSON from the synced repo before it re-propagates. Step 3 (hunt): Identify the sync repo/owner who introduced the row and every peer device consuming it; run UC1 across those hosts and review who had write access to the shared workspace.
let AVWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
    | where FileName endswith ".json"
    | project AVWriteTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AVFile = FolderPath, AVWriter = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "siyuan"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project SpawnTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| join kind=inner AVWrites on DeviceId
| where SpawnTime between (AVWriteTime .. AVWriteTime + 5m)   // shell spawns within 5m of an AV-cell JSON write
| project AVWriteTime, SpawnTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SpawnTime, AVWriteTime), DeviceName, AccountName, AVFile, AVWriter, ChildImage, ChildCmd
| order by SpawnTime desc

Second-stage egress from SiYuan-spawned LOLBin (post-RCE ingress tool transfer) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the download/C2 tail of the SiYuan XSS-to-RCE: a process spawned by SiYuan.exe (cmd/powershell/certutil/curl/bitsadmin etc.) making an outbound connection to a public IP. Distinct network pivot from the process-spawn detection — catches payloads whose only host action is second-stage retrieval or beaconing. Rationale: Reuses the confirmed SiYuan.exe parent boundary but pivots on the network layer (InitiatingProcessParentFileName + public RemoteIP), catching the ingress-tool-transfer step the process-spawn rule alone would miss; Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog left empty because the process-to-network grandparent link (child spawned by SiYuan) is only reliably carried in DeviceNetworkEvents and the Falcon ProcessRollup2->NetworkConnectIP4 join. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://dailycve.com/siyuan-stored-xss-to-rce-critical/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan spawning curl/powershell for a legitimate plugin or bundled updater fetching over HTTPS
  • rundll32 launched by SiYuan to open an external link, resolving the target site
  • Corporate proxy/inspection appliance rewriting the SiYuan-spawned connection to a public sinkhole
  • Admin manually testing SiYuan integrations from a shell that was, by coincidence, launched from the app
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "rundll32.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "FileProtocolHandler")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve RemoteIP/RemoteUrl reputation and inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine for download verbs (certutil -urlcache, curl/wget http, bitsadmin /transfer, IWR/DownloadString). Unknown/newly-registered destination + download verb = true positive. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block the destination IP/domain at egress, and capture the fetched artifact for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all peers of the same SiYuan sync workspace for connections to the same destination, and pivot the retrieved second-stage hash across the estate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName startswith "siyuan"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: File Browser Hook-Auth Command Injection - filebrowser Spawns Shell or Recon Binary

description: Detects the File Browser server binary spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child, indicative of CVE-2026-54088 pre-auth command injection via the authentication hook.
references:

  - https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10

detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '/filebrowser'
  tool_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/id'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/uname'
      - '/hostname'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/socat'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'

  shell_child:

      - '/etc/passwd'
      - '/etc/shadow'

      - ';'
      - '$('
  condition: parent and (tool_child or (shell_child and shell_markers))
level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^filebrowser$/i
| (ImageFileName=/\/(id|whoami|uname|hostname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|python[0-9]?|perl|ruby|php)$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|ash|zsh|ksh)$/i AND regex("(/etc/passwd|/etc/shadow|whoami|uname|/dev/tcp/|;|\\$\\()", field=CommandLine)))

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="filebrowser" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh") AND (Processes.process="*/etc/passwd*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/shadow*" OR Processes.process="*whoami*" OR Processes.process="*uname*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/tcp/*" OR Processes.process="*;*" OR Processes.process="*`*" OR Processes.process="*$(*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser /api/login carrying forged X-Remote-User / X-Auth proxy-auth header AIExploitation High
Hunts POST requests to the FileBrowser /api/login endpoint that carry a proxy-auth identity header (e.g. X-Remote-User) but originate from a source other than the trusted reverse proxy. CVE-2026-54089 lets any client that reaches FileBrowser directly forge this header to be minted an admin JWT with no password check. Rationale: Anchors on the FileBrowser-specific /api/login API path (the endpoint that reaches ProxyAuth.Auth), surfacing source IP so an analyst can spot logins arriving from anything other than the reverse proxy. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory and the filebrowser auth/proxy.go source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/main/auth/proxy.go • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=filebrowser
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SSO users authenticating through the reverse proxy (their src IP will be the proxy)
  • Health-check / uptime monitors hitting /api/login on a schedule
  • CI/CD or backup jobs that authenticate to FileBrowser via API
  • Load balancer synthetic probes originating from an internal VIP
  • Admin troubleshooting the login flow directly from the host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source IP is the sanctioned reverse proxy (nginx/Traefik/Caddy/Apache). Any /api/login POST from a non-proxy IP on a proxy-auth deployment is suspect; inspect the raw request for an X-Remote-User / X-Auth header. 2) Contain: firewall the FileBrowser port so only the proxy IP can reach it (bind to 127.0.0.1), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any forged admin tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate all users in the FileBrowser DB for accounts created out-of-band and review /api/settings, /api/users and file-download activity from the offending source.

| where RemoteIPType == "Public"

| order by Connections desc
ImWebSession

| order by LoginAttempts desc

FileBrowser auto-provisioning abuse: burst of distinct usernames via forged proxy header AIInstallation Medium
Detects a burst of /api/login POSTs from a single source in a short window, indicating exploitation of CVE-2026-54089's account-creation primitive where a forged header naming a non-existent user causes FileBrowser to auto-create that account. Multiple new usernames from one client is high-confidence provisioning abuse. Rationale: The article states a non-existent username auto-creates an account with no opt-in; each forged login with a fresh username persists a new user. A 10-in-10-minutes burst from one source is a strong provisioning-abuse signal that clean SSO traffic never produces. Corroborated via the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/main/auth/proxy.go
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy SSO proxy funnelling many real users' first-time logins through one proxy egress IP (mitigate by excluding the proxy IP)
  • Automated login/health probes retrying rapidly
  • A pentest or vulnerability scanner enumerating the endpoint
  • Mobile clients retrying auth on flaky networks
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FileBrowser user DB (or app logs) and list accounts whose creation timestamp aligns with the burst window; the auto-created accounts carry LockPassword=true and default permissions. 2) Contain: delete the rogue accounts, restrict the FileBrowser port to the proxy, and rotate the JWT signing key. 3) Hunt: review what each new account did (file downloads, /api/settings changes) and check whether default permissions granted execute/create capabilities that were abused.

FileBrowser admin endpoint access from session lacking legitimate admin login AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts write/delete actions against FileBrowser admin-only endpoints (/api/settings, /api/users, /api/resources) grouped by source, to surface a client exercising admin capability obtained through the CVE-2026-54089 forged-header bypass rather than a genuine credentialed admin session. Rationale: The bypass mints an admin JWT, so post-exploit activity shows up as writes to FileBrowser's admin-only API paths named in the article's attack flow. Grouping by source lets an analyst separate the sanctioned proxy from a direct attacker. Cross-checked with the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm

Response runbook
1) Triage: verify whether the source IP is the reverse proxy and whether a legitimate admin session existed; a /api/settings or /api/users write from a non-proxy IP on a proxy-auth deployment is the tell. 2) Contain: revoke sessions by rotating the JWT signing key, restrict the FileBrowser port to the proxy, and review recent settings/user changes for tampering. 3) Hunt: diff current settings and user list against a known-good baseline, and pivot on the same source IP across /api/login and file-download telemetry.

Direct inbound connection to FileBrowser port bypassing the reverse proxy AIDelivery High
Detects inbound TCP connections to the exposed FileBrowser listener (example port 8085 from the advisory PoC) from public / non-proxy sources. A proxy-auth deployment should have all traffic fronted by the reverse proxy, so any direct external connection is the precondition for the CVE-2026-54089 header-forgery bypass. Rationale: The advisory PoC publishes the container on port 8085 (-p 8085:80) and states direct reachability is the sole exploit prerequisite; a proxy-auth deployment should see zero non-proxy inbound to that port. Operators should adjust the port to their published value. Corroborated with the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1199 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The reverse proxy itself connecting to the backend (allowlist the proxy IP)
  • Local health checks / monitoring agents on the same host or subnet
  • Container orchestration probes (Kubernetes liveness/readiness) hitting the port
  • An admin deliberately connecting for debugging as noted in the advisory
  • Internal vulnerability scanners sweeping the port
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileBrowser deployment uses auth.method=proxy and identify whether the connecting source is the sanctioned reverse proxy; anything else reaching the port directly can forge auth. 2) Contain: rebind FileBrowser to 127.0.0.1 or firewall the port so only the proxy IP can connect, then rotate the JWT signing key. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IP with /api/login POSTs and admin-endpoint writes in the same window, and audit the user DB for auto-created accounts.

Chromium browser connecting to SiYuan kernel loopback API (127.0.0.1:6806) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a standalone Chrome/Chromium/Edge browser process opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan kernel HTTP server on port 6806. Under CVE-2026-54069 the kernel grants RoleAdministrator to any chrome-extension:// origin with no auth, so a browser (not the SiYuan Electron shell) driving traffic to 6806 is the exploitation channel for an unauthorized extension. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article artifacts — loopback 127.0.0.1 + port 6806 (SiYuan default kernel port, corroborated) driven by a browser process, which is precisely how a malicious/compromised chrome-extension reaches the auth-bypassed admin API. Kept as hunting because SiYuan officially supports browser access to 6806 and ships a legitimate extension. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069 • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/blob/master/API.md • https://chromeboard.com/extension/siyuan-hkcgjbeblifaincobbcfiffbpgoafepk
ATT&CKT1176 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately opening SiYuan in a browser tab at http://127.0.0.1:6806 (officially supported access mode).
  • The official SiYuan web-clipper Chrome extension (id hkcgjbeblifaincobbcfiffbpgoafepk) syncing clips to the local kernel.
  • Developers/power users testing the SiYuan API via a browser-based REST client or DevTools console.
  • Localhost port scanners or security tooling (e.g., browser-based localhost enumeration extensions) probing 6806.
  • Browser-embedded automation/e2e frameworks (Selenium/Playwright driving Chrome) hitting a local SiYuan instance in CI.
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the browser and, if endpoint supports it, the extension inventory on the host (chrome://extensions / registry \Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions). Confirm whether SiYuan version is <= 3.6.5 (vulnerable). Check if the traffic pattern is a one-off UI load vs sustained programmatic bursts. 2) Contain: If an unknown/unexpected extension is present, disable/remove it and treat browser profile as suspect; upgrade SiYuan to >= 3.7.0 which removes the blanket allowlist. 3) Hunt: Pivot to SiYuan.exe outbound connections to new external hosts (stored-XSS exfil) and to any note content containing 'onerror' img payloads or unexpected /api/system/setConf changes.
DeviceNetworkEvents

SiYuan renderer beaconing to first-seen external host (stored-XSS cookie exfil) AIActions on Objectives Low
Detects the SiYuan desktop process making an outbound connection to a public host it has never contacted in the baseline window. CVE-2026-54069 allows an extension to inject a stored-XSS payload (img onerror fetching to an attacker URL with document.cookie) via /api/block/insertBlock, which fires inside the SiYuan renderer and beacons out. Rationale: The article's PoC step 3 injects an img/onerror payload that fetches to an external URL carrying document.cookie; that fetch executes in the SiYuan (Electron) renderer, so a first-seen external destination for siyuan.exe is the observable tail of the stored-XSS exfil. Low confidence because SiYuan's own cloud-sync traffic is a legitimate external destination. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3 • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan cloud sync / subscription service connecting to siyuan.io or its S3/OSS storage backend for the first time after setup.
  • SiYuan update checks or plugin marketplace downloads reaching a new CDN endpoint.
  • User embedding a remote image/asset in a note, causing the renderer to fetch a legitimate external host.
  • Third-party SiYuan plugins that legitimately call external APIs from the renderer.
  • Baseline gap: a newly provisioned host with < 30 days of history flags every normal destination as first-seen.
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "siyuan.io" and RemoteUrl !endswith "b3logfile.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect the new external destination — resolve the domain, check reputation, and confirm it is not siyuan.io/official sync or a known plugin endpoint. Look for URL query strings resembling cookie/token exfil (e.g. ?data=). 2) Contain: If the destination is malicious, block it at proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and rotate any credentials that may have been in document.cookie for the SiYuan session. 3) Hunt: Search recent /api/block/insertBlock or /api/attr/setBlockAttrs activity and grep the workspace for note blocks containing 'onerror=' or 'fetch(' to find the injected stored-XSS payload; enumerate installed browser extensions on the host.

SiYuan kernel listening on 6806 — vulnerable-config exposure inventory AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt that surfaces every host where SiYuan.exe binds a listening socket on port 6806, projecting the product version so analysts can flag installs <= 3.6.5 that carry the CVE-2026-54069 blanket chrome-extension:// allowlist. Confirms exploitable surface rather than active exploitation. Rationale: Uses the SiYuan.exe binary + fixed kernel port 6806 (corroborated as the default) and the ListeningConnectionCreated action to enumerate exploitable installs, projecting InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion to distinguish vulnerable (<=3.6.5) from patched (>=3.7.0) hosts. High-fidelity as a low-noise asset/config hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069 • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/blob/master/API.md
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched SiYuan hosts (>= 3.7.0) still listen on 6806 but are not vulnerable — version projection is the discriminator, not the listener itself.
  • SiYuan running in a container/server publish mode where the port is deliberately exposed and an AccessAuthCode is set.
  • Non-SiYuan software coincidentally binding 6806 (rare; the InitiatingProcessFileName filter removes these).
  • Loopback-only telemetry gaps on some EDR agent versions may under-report listeners (false negatives, not positives).
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each host, read the projected SiYuanVersion; anything <= 3.6.5 is exploitable. Confirm whether AccessAuthCode is empty (desktop default) which fully removes token validation. 2) Contain: Push SiYuan upgrade to >= 3.7.0 org-wide; where upgrade is delayed, set a non-empty AccessAuthCode and restrict browser-extension install policy via managed Chrome/Edge ADMX. 3) Hunt: On vulnerable hosts, review UC-1 (browser→6806) and UC-2 (siyuan.exe external beacon) hits over the same window, and audit note content for injected onerror/fetch stored-XSS payloads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort == 6806
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LocalIP, LocalPort, SiYuanVersion=InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion
| extend LikelyVulnerable = iff(isnotempty(SiYuanVersion) and SiYuanVersion !startswith "3.7" and SiYuanVersion !startswith "3.8" and SiYuanVersion !startswith "3.9" and SiYuanVersion !startswith "4.", "review (<=3.6.5 is vulnerable)", "check version")
| order by LastSeen desc

Authorizer /authorize implicit-flow token leak via unvalidated redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the Authorizer /authorize endpoint using the implicit flow (response_type=token or id_token) that carry a redirect_uri, and surfaces the redirect_uri host for allowlist comparison. The vulnerable handler appends access_token/id_token/refresh_token and 302-redirects to any attacker-supplied URL, so an off-origin redirect_uri on the implicit flow is the exploitation signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (/authorize), the implicit-flow trigger (response_type=token / id_token) and the redirect_uri parameter that lacks IsValidOrigin() validation; projects the decoded redirect_uri host so an analyst can compare it against the deployment's AllowedOrigins. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately registered SPA client using the implicit flow with a redirect_uri that IS in AllowedOrigins
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, ZAP) probing /authorize during authorized pentests
  • Internal QA/staging traffic pointing redirect_uri at test hostnames
  • Legacy first-party app still on implicit flow before migration to auth-code+PKCE
Suppression filter
| where redirect_host !in~ ("your-authorizer-host.example.com")   // analyst: replace with AllowedOrigins hostnames
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract redirect_host from the hit and compare against the Authorizer AllowedOrigins config; an off-origin/attacker domain confirms exploitation. Check scStatus for 302 and the source IP/user-agent. 2) Contain: patch Authorizer to a build >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d (adds IsValidOrigin on /authorize); if patching is delayed, block implicit-flow response_types at the WAF and force affected users to reset sessions/rotate refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot on the redirect_host and any recon of /graphql {meta{client_id}} from the same IP, and review /userinfo access with tokens shortly after the redirect to spot token replay.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| where Url has "response_type=token" or Url has "response_type=id_token"
| where Url has "redirect_uri="
| extend redirect_uri = url_decode(extract(@"redirect_uri=([^&]+)", 1, Url))
| extend redirect_host = tolower(extract(@"^https?://([^/]+)", 1, redirect_uri))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, redirect_host, redirect_uri, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
